title: Bonds absorb infrared radiation by vibrating
keyIdea: A covalent bond behaves like a spring between two masses: it stretches and bends at its own natural frequency, which lies in the infrared. In the ball-and-spring model the wavenumber is proportional to √(k/μ): a stronger bond (larger force constant k) vibrates faster, so C≡O > C=O > C–O, and heavier atoms (larger reduced mass μ) vibrate more slowly, so C–H ≈ 3000, C–D ≈ 2200 and C–Cl ≈ 800 cm⁻¹. Vibrational energy comes in fixed steps, so a bond absorbs only infrared photons whose frequency matches its vibration, which is why each bond has characteristic absorptions. A vibration absorbs only if it changes the molecule's dipole: N₂ and O₂ do not absorb, but CO₂ (bend and asymmetric stretch), H₂O and CH₄ do, so they absorb infrared given out by the warm Earth and act as greenhouse gases.
familyTip: Hold a ruler at one end and twang it, then hold it further along to make it shorter and stiffer. Talk about why the stiffer ruler vibrates faster, and how a bond is like a tiny, very stiff spring.

visual.caption: Does this vibration absorb infrared? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pluck spring bonds (mass and strength set the wavenumber), tune IR until C=O absorbs, sort vibrations by dipole change, find greenhouse gases.

kid: Picture a covalent bond as a spring with a ball at each end. The atoms are never still. The bond stretches and squashes, and it can also bend. Each bond does this at its own speed, called its natural frequency. For bonds, that speed falls in the infrared part of the spectrum.

Two things set the speed. A stiff spring snaps back fast, so a strong bond vibrates fast. A triple bond beats a double bond, and a double bond beats a single bond. Heavy balls move slowly, so heavy atoms vibrate slowly. That is why C–H, with its light H atom, absorbs near 3000 cm⁻¹, but C–Cl absorbs near 800 cm⁻¹.

A bond cannot take any amount of energy. Its vibration energy goes up in fixed steps. So it only takes in a photon whose energy is just one step. That means it absorbs IR at its own frequency, and the rest passes by. This is why each kind of bond has its own place in an IR spectrum.

There is one more rule. IR is a field that flips to and fro, so it can only push on a charge that shifts. The vibration must change the dipole. N₂ and O₂ have the same atom at each end, so they never do. CO₂, water and methane do. They take in the IR given out by the warm ground. That is why they are greenhouse gases.
adult: Ages 16 to 18. This covers AQA A-level Chemistry 3.3.6.2 (bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers, and the link between IR absorption by CO₂, methane and water vapour and global warming) and OCR A 4.2.4. The ball-and-spring formula ν̃ = (1/2πc)√(k/μ) is beyond the specifications but explains the data-book pattern; the lab's values come from it and sit inside the AQA data sheet ranges.

The lab has five tasks. Learners pluck C–H, C–D and C–Cl to see mass lower the wavenumber, then C–O, C=O and C≡O to see bond strength raise it. They tune an IR source until the C=O bond absorbs at about 1710 cm⁻¹. They sort seven vibrations by whether the dipole changes, and find which gases in air trap the infrared given out by the ground.

Common mistakes. Students often think IR absorption breaks bonds or moves electrons, that every bond absorbs, or that longer bonds absorb at higher wavenumbers. Many say N₂ does not absorb because its bond is strong, when the reason is that no dipole change occurs. Some think a molecule must be polar to absorb, yet non-polar CO₂ absorbs through its bend and asymmetric stretch.

practice.prompt: Why does C=O absorb at a higher wavenumber than C–O?
choices: The double bond is stronger, a stiffer spring
The O atom is heavier in C=O
practice.hint: Same atoms, so only the spring changes.
practice.explain: C=O has a larger force constant than C–O. A stiffer spring vibrates faster, so C=O absorbs near 1700 cm⁻¹ and C–O near 1000–1300 cm⁻¹.

practice.prompt: In the ball-and-spring model the wavenumber is proportional to √k. The force constant is made {=n*n} times bigger with the same atoms. By what factor does the wavenumber rise?
practice.hint: Wavenumber goes with the square root of k, so take the square root of the factor.
practice.explain: √{=n*n} = {n}. Making the spring {=n*n} times stiffer only makes it vibrate {n} times faster.

practice.prompt: Which gas does not absorb infrared radiation given out by the Earth?
practice.hint: Which molecule has the same atom at both ends of its only bond?
practice.explain: Stretching N≡N never changes the dipole, so IR cannot drive it. CO₂ and CH₄ have vibrations that change the dipole, so they absorb.

practice.prompt: A bond absorbs at {n}00 cm⁻¹. If the reduced mass were 4 times larger with the same spring, at what wavenumber (cm⁻¹) would it absorb?
practice.explain: √4 = 2, so the wavenumber halves: {n}00 ÷ 2 = {=n*50} cm⁻¹. More mass, slower vibration. (Swapping H for D in C–H raises μ by about 1.86, so 3000 falls to about 2200 cm⁻¹.)

practice.prompt: A bond vibrates at 1715 cm⁻¹. Infrared of all wavenumbers is shone at it. What happens?
choices: Only IR near 1715 cm⁻¹ is absorbed
All of the IR is absorbed equally
practice.hint: Vibrational energy comes in fixed steps.
practice.explain: Only photons whose energy matches one vibrational step, near 1715 cm⁻¹, are absorbed. The bond vibrates harder; it does not break.

pool.prompt: Which bond absorbs at the lowest wavenumber?
pool.hint: Heavy atoms and weaker bonds both lower the frequency.
pool.explain: Cl is heavy and C–Cl is weaker than C=O, so C–Cl absorbs at about 550–850 cm⁻¹, below C=O (about 1700) and C–H (about 3000).

pool.prompt: CO₂ is non-polar. Why can it still absorb infrared?
choices: Its bend and asymmetric stretch make a dipole appear
pool.hint: Think about the dipole during the vibration, not at rest.
pool.explain: At rest CO₂ has no dipole, but bending or stretching one bond more than the other creates one for a moment, so IR can drive those vibrations.

pool.prompt: What does a bond gain when it absorbs an infrared photon?
pool.explain: An IR photon raises the bond to a higher vibrational level. It is far too weak to break the bond or move electrons to a new orbital.

pool.prompt: A bond absorbs at {n}00 cm⁻¹. If its force constant were 4 times larger, with the same atoms, at what wavenumber (cm⁻¹) would it absorb?
pool.explain: √4 = 2, so the wavenumber doubles: {n}00 × 2 = {=n*200} cm⁻¹. Real bonds change less: C≡O (about 2140) has about 1.6 times the force constant of C=O (about 1700).

pool.prompt: Why is O–H absorption at a higher wavenumber than C–O absorption?
choices: H is very light, so O–H vibrates fast
O–H contains oxygen, which is heavy
pool.hint: What does a light ball on a spring do?
pool.explain: The light H atom gives O–H a small reduced mass, so it vibrates fast and absorbs near 3200–3600 cm⁻¹. C–O has two heavy atoms and absorbs near 1000–1300 cm⁻¹.

pool.hint: In which one do the two bond dipoles stay equal and opposite?
pool.explain: In the symmetric stretch both C=O bonds lengthen together, so the dipoles still cancel and nothing changes. The bends create or change a dipole.

pool.prompt: A wavenumber of {n}00 cm⁻¹ means {n}00 waves fit in 1 cm. How many of these waves fit in 1 mm?
pool.hint: 1 mm is a tenth of 1 cm, so a tenth as many waves fit in it.
pool.explain: {n}00 ÷ 10 = {=n*10} waves in 1 mm. More waves per cm means a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency and photon energy.

pool.prompt: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99% of dry air. Why are they not greenhouse gases?
choices: Their vibrations never change the dipole
Their bonds are too weak to vibrate
pool.hint: Both are made of two identical atoms.
pool.explain: A diatomic molecule of two identical atoms has no dipole at any stretch, so IR cannot drive the vibration and the gas lets the Earth's IR pass.

pool.prompt: Why does each type of bond show absorptions at its own characteristic wavenumbers?
choices: Each has its own force constant and atom masses
All bonds vibrate at the same frequency
The wavenumber depends only on the molecule's size
pool.hint: What two things set a spring's frequency?
pool.explain: Bond strength (force constant) and the masses of the atoms set the frequency, so C–H, O–H, C=O and C–O each absorb in their own range.
